verses.sanskrit: असतो मा सद्गमय | तमसो मा ज्योतिर्गमय | मृत्योर्मामृतं गमय | ॐ शान्तिः शान्तिः शान्तिः ||
verses.transliteration: asato mā sadgamaya | tamaso mā jyotirgamaya | mṛtyormā amṛtaṃ gamaya | oṃ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ ||
verses.translation: Lead me from the unreal to the Real. Lead me from darkness to Light. Lead me from death to Immortality. OM — Peace, Peace, Peace.
verses.hindi: असत् (मिथ्या) से सत् (सत्य) की ओर ले चलो। अंधकार से प्रकाश की ओर ले चलो। मृत्यु से अमृत की ओर ले चलो। ॐ शान्तिः शान्तिः शान्तिः।
verses.commentary: One of the most universally resonant prayers ever composed. It does not pray for things — wealth, health, power — but for transformation of consciousness: from falsehood to truth, from ignorance to wisdom, from mortality to immortality. These three pairs describe the entire spiritual journey. The prayer acknowledges: I am currently in unreal, dark, mortal perception — and asks for guidance beyond it.

verses.sanskrit: एकं सद्विप्रा बहुधा वदन्ति अग्निं यमं मातरिश्वानमाहुः ||
verses.transliteration: ekaṃ sadvipra bahudhā vadanti agniṃ yamaṃ mātariśvānamāhuḥ ||
verses.translation: Truth is one; the wise call it by many names — Agni, Yama, Matarishvan.
verses.hindi: सत् (सत्य) एक ही है; विद्वान उसे अनेक नामों से पुकारते हैं — अग्नि, यम, मातरिश्वा आदि।
verses.commentary: The most celebrated verse in the Rig Veda — the philosophical foundation of Hindu pluralism. "Ekam Sat Vipra Bahudha Vadanti" — Reality is one; wise people describe it in many ways. All the gods, all the religions, all the spiritual paths are different names for the one truth. No tradition has a monopoly. This is not relativism (all views are equal) but pluralism (one truth, many valid approaches).

verses.sanskrit: अग्ने नय सुपथा राये अस्मान् विश्वानि देव वयुनानि विद्वान् | युयोध्यस्मज्जुहुराणमेनो भूयिष्ठां ते नम उक्तिं विधेम ||
verses.transliteration: agne naya supathā rāye asmān viśvāni deva vayunāni vidvān | yuyodhyasmajjuhurāṇameno bhūyiṣṭhāṃ te nama uktiṃ vidhema ||
verses.translation: O Agni, lead us by the good path to prosperity. O God, you know all our deeds. Remove the sin that leads us astray. We offer you the most abundant words of homage.
verses.hindi: हे अग्नि, हमें उत्तम मार्ग से सम्पदा की ओर ले चलो। हे देव, तुम हमारे सभी कर्म जानते हो। हमें भटकाने वाले पाप को दूर करो। हम तुम्हें सर्वाधिक नमन के शब्द अर्पित करते हैं।
verses.commentary: This verse appears in both Mandala 2 and as the closing verse of the Isha Upanishad (18) — one of the most significant convergences in the tradition. "Agne naya supathā" — O Agni, lead us by the good path. The prayer is not for wealth directly but for the path to wealth — the right way to prosperity, not the crooked way. "Vayunāni vidvān" — you know all our deeds: Agni as the internal witness, the fire of conscience that sees every action. "Juhurāṇam eno" — the crooked sin, the deviation from Rita. The verse closes with the most complete offering: not gold or animals but "nama-ukti" — the words of homage themselves, offered in abundance.

verses.sanskrit: ऋतस्य पन्था न दभाय किं चन वृजिना ह्यस्य नश्यन्ति जन्तवः | ऋतेन दीर्घमनु वेनतो दिवः पदं न दुष्कृते अपि तं नशे ||
verses.transliteration: ṛtasya panthā na dabhāya kiṃ cana vṛjinā hyasya naśyanti jantavaḥ | ṛtena dīrghamanu venato divaḥ padaṃ na duṣkṛte api taṃ naśe ||
verses.translation: The path of Rita cannot be deceived by anyone. Those who follow crooked ways perish. By Rita the vast luminous realm is reached — the evildoer cannot attain that place.
verses.hindi: ऋत के मार्ग को कोई धोखा नहीं दे सकता। वक्र पथ पर चलने वाले नष्ट हो जाते हैं। ऋत से ही वह विशाल द्युलोक प्राप्त होता है — दुष्कर्मी उसे नहीं पा सकता।
verses.commentary: The Rig Veda's most direct statement of Rita — the cosmic ordering principle that is simultaneously physical law and moral law. "Ṛtasya panthā na dabhāya kiṃ cana" — the path of cosmic order cannot be deceived by anyone. Gravity does not make exceptions. Truth does not make exceptions. Rita maintains the three worlds — earth, atmosphere, heaven. The moral implication: human actions that conform to Rita produce flourishing; those that violate it produce destruction. Not as divine punishment but as the natural consequence of acting against the structure of reality itself.

verses.sanskrit: सहस्रशीर्षा पुरुषः सहस्राक्षः सहस्रपात् | स भूमिं विश्वतो वृत्वात्यतिष्ठद्दशाङ्गुलम् ||
verses.transliteration: sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ sahasrākṣaḥ sahasrapāt | sa bhūmiṃ viśvato vṛtvātyatiṣṭhaddaśāṅgulam ||
verses.translation: The Cosmic Person has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet. He pervades the earth on all sides and stands ten fingers beyond.
verses.hindi: पुरुष (विराट्) के हज़ार सिर, हज़ार आँखें और हज़ार पैर हैं। वह सब ओर से पृथ्वी को व्याप्त करके दस अंगुल अतिक्रमण करके स्थित है।
verses.commentary: The Purusha Sukta (RV 10.90) presents the universe as a single vast Conscious Being — not as dead matter arranged by chance but as a living, integrated whole. "Thousand heads, eyes, feet" is not literal; it conveys omniscience, omnipresence, and infinite diversity within one consciousness. The universe is not a machine; it is a Person — aware, unified, complete.

verses.sanskrit: विमुचेन्यसि वरुण पाशान् यैरबद्धो असि जातवेदः | यद्धि ते विश्वमनुमत्यम्भिर्वयं सुमित्राः स्याम ||
verses.transliteration: vimucenya si varuṇa pāśān yairabaddho asi jātavedaḥ | yaddhi te viśvamanumatyambhirvayaṃ sumitrāḥ syāma ||
verses.translation: Release, O Varuna, the bonds with which I am bound, O Jataveda. For by your will, O all-knowing one — may we be among your good friends.
verses.hindi: हे वरुण, उन बन्धनों से मुझे मुक्त करो जिनसे मैं बँधा हूँ, हे जातवेद। क्योंकि तुम्हारी इच्छा से ही — हम तुम्हारे सुमित्र हों।
verses.commentary: The culminating prayer of the Varuna sequence: "vimucenya si varuṇa pāśān" — release, O Varuna, the bonds. The Vedic concept of pāśa (bonds, fetters) — the same root that gives the word "pashu" (bound creature) in Shaiva Tantra. The bonds are not external chains but the interior constrictions produced by unresolved transgression: guilt, shame, the habitual contraction around what one has done or left undone. The prayer moves from "what did I do wrong?" (7.86.1) to "release the bonds" — acknowledging that whatever the transgression was, its effect is a constraint on life-force itself. "Sumitrāḥ syāma" — may we be your good friends. The relationship with the divine, having been fractured by transgression, seeks restoration.

verses.sanskrit: इन्द्रो मायाभिः पुरुरूप ईयते युक्ता ह्यस्य हरयः शता दश | आयं शक्र इत्येनमाहुर्यः स्वर्षाता सत्पतिः शूरो अस्तु ||
verses.transliteration: indro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate yuktā hyasya harayaḥ śatā daśa | āyaṃ śakra ityenamāhuryaḥ svarṣātā satpatiḥ śūro astu ||
verses.translation: Indra moves in many forms through his powers of maya. His golden coursers are yoked a thousand and ten. They call him Shakra — may he who wins the heavenly light, lord of the good, be heroic.
verses.hindi: इन्द्र अपनी माया-शक्तियों से अनेक रूप धारण करके विचरते हैं। उनके दस सौ सुनहरे अश्व जुते हैं। उन्हें शक्र कहते हैं — जो स्वर्ग-प्रकाश प्राप्त करे, सत्पुरुषों का स्वामी, वह शूर हो।
verses.commentary: This verse introduces one of the Rig Veda's most philosophically rich concepts: Vedic "māyā" — not yet in its later Vedantic sense of "illusion" but in its original sense of "creative power, the capacity to take many forms." Indra's māyā is his ability to appear in multiple forms simultaneously — the power of infinite self-expression. "Pururūpa" — many-formed. The thousand golden coursers are the infinite forces through which the cosmic principle of Indra manifests. This verse anticipates the Vedantic māyā doctrine: the one reality appears as the many through the creative power of self-differentiation.

verses.sanskrit: मरुतो यद्ध वो बलं यच्च सत्यमुत क्रतुः | तेन मा पातनाधसः ||
verses.transliteration: maruto yadha vo balaṃ yacca satyamuta kratuḥ | tena mā pātanādhasaḥ ||
verses.translation: O Maruts — whatever strength you have, whatever truth, whatever purposeful will — by that, protect me from falling low.
verses.hindi: हे मरुतो — तुम्हारे पास जो बल है, जो सत्य है, जो संकल्पशक्ति है — उससे मुझे नीचे गिरने से बचाओ।
verses.commentary: The Maruts are the storm-gods — the vital winds, the forces of prana that move through the cosmos and through the body. They are "bala" (strength), "satya" (truth), and "kratu" (purposeful will — the capacity to act with decisive intention). The prayer asks to be protected from "adhas" — falling low, sinking, degradation. The Maruts' three qualities are exactly what prevents that fall: physical vitality (bala) to sustain the body, truth (satya) to orient perception accurately, and purposeful will (kratu) to act from genuine intention rather than reactive impulse. The Vedic model of resilience: not the absence of storms but having the storm-energy itself as your ally.

verses.sanskrit: तत्सवितुर्वरेण्यं भर्गो देवस्य धीमहि | धियो यो नः प्रचोदयात् ||
verses.transliteration: tatsaviturvareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi | dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt ||
verses.translation: We meditate on the excellent glory of the divine Savitar; may he illuminate our intellects.
verses.hindi: हम उस देव सविता के श्रेष्ठ तेज का ध्यान करते हैं। वह हमारी बुद्धि (धी) को प्रेरित करे।
verses.commentary: The Gayatri Mantra (RV 3.62.10) is the most sacred and most widely recited mantra in the Vedic tradition. Savitar is the divine Impeller — the force that sets everything in motion, that drives intelligence itself. This is not a prayer for material things but for intellectual illumination: "May the light of the cosmic intelligence enter my mind." It is the Vedic prayer of the scientist, the philosopher, and the seeker.

verses.sanskrit: एक एव अग्निर्बहुधा समिद्धः एकः सूर्यो विश्वमनु प्रभूतः | एकैवोषाः सर्वमिदं विभाति एकं वा इदं विबभूव सर्वम् ||
verses.transliteration: eka eva agnirbahudha samiddhaḥ ekaḥ sūryo viśvamanu prabhūtaḥ | ekaivoṣāḥ sarvamidaṃ vibhāti ekaṃ vā idaṃ vibabhūva sarvam ||
verses.translation: Fire is one, kindled in many ways. The Sun is one, pervading the whole world. The Dawn is one — she illumines all this. The One alone has become all this.
verses.hindi: अग्नि एक ही है, अनेक प्रकार से प्रज्वलित। सूर्य एक ही है, सारे जगत् में व्याप्त। उषा एक ही है — वह सब को प्रकाशित करती है। वास्तव में यह सब वही एक है।
verses.commentary: The Vishvamitra Mandala contains more than the Gayatri — it also articulates the philosophical monism that the Gayatri presupposes. This verse states it plainly: the light of Agni, the light of Surya, the light of Ushas — one light, one source, one reality. "Ekaṃ vā idaṃ vibabhūva sarvam" — the One alone has become all this. This is the metaphysics underlying the Gayatri mantra: when you meditate on the "bhargo devasya" — the divine light of Savitar — you are not addressing a separate deity; you are recognising the single light that is the ground of all perception. The Mandala that gives us the Gayatri also gives us the understanding of why it works: the light you seek to enter your mind is the same light as your mind itself. Ekam Sat Vipra Bahudha Vadanti (RV 1.164.46) — truth is one; the wise speak of it in many ways — finds its cosmological expression here.

verses.sanskrit: अहं मनुरभवं सूर्यश्चाहमहं ककुहः ऋषिरस्मि विप्रः | अहमिन्द्रो नॄन्नमसा विवक्मि ||
verses.transliteration: ahaṃ manurabhaваṃ sūryaścāhaṃ kakuhaḥ ṛṣirasmi vipraḥ | ahamindro nṝnnamasā vivakmi ||
verses.translation: I was Manu; I was Surya. I am the seer Kakuha; I am the illumined poet. I am Indra — I declare this to humanity with homage.
verses.hindi: मैं मनु था; मैं सूर्य था। मैं ऋषि ककुह हूँ; मैं विप्र (ज्ञानी) हूँ। मैं इन्द्र हूँ — मैं नमन के साथ मनुष्यों से यह घोषित करता हूँ।
verses.commentary: RV 4.26.1 — the most stunning non-dual declaration in the Rig Veda. Vamadeva speaks in a state of direct realisation: "Ahaṃ manurabhaваṃ" — I was Manu, the first human, the archetype of humanity. "Sūryaścāhaṃ" — I was Surya, the Sun itself. "Ahamindro" — I am Indra, king of the gods. The Aitareya Upanishad (2.1.5) uses this verse as the paradigm case of direct identity-knowledge — the realisation that atman and brahman are not separate. The sage does not say "I am united with" or "I am similar to" — he says "I am." The "aham" that was Manu and Surya is not the personal ego of Vamadeva; it is the universal "I" that is the ground of all individuated awareness.

verses.transliteration: sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ sahasrākṣaḥ sahasrapāt | sa bhūmiṃ viśvato vṛtvātyatiṣṭhaddaśāṅgulam ||
verses.translation: The Cosmic Person has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet. He pervades the earth on all sides and stands ten fingers beyond.
verses.hindi: पुरुष (विराट्) के हज़ार सिर, हज़ार आँखें और हज़ार पैर हैं। वह सब ओर से पृथ्वी को व्याप्त करके दस अंगुल अतिक्रमण करके स्थित है।
verses.commentary: The Purusha Sukta (RV 10.90) presents the universe as a single vast Conscious Being — not as dead matter arranged by chance but as a living, integrated whole. "Thousand heads, eyes, feet" is not literal; it conveys omniscience, omnipresence, and infinite diversity within one consciousness. The universe is not a machine; it is a Person — aware, unified, complete.

verses.sanskrit: विमुचेन्यसि वरुण पाशान् यैरबद्धो असि जातवेदः | यद्धि ते विश्वमनुमत्यम्भिर्वयं सुमित्राः स्याम ||
verses.transliteration: vimucenya si varuṇa pāśān yairabaddho asi jātavedaḥ | yaddhi te viśvamanumatyambhirvayaṃ sumitrāḥ syāma ||
verses.translation: Release, O Varuna, the bonds with which I am bound, O Jataveda. For by your will, O all-knowing one — may we be among your good friends.
verses.hindi: हे वरुण, उन बन्धनों से मुझे मुक्त करो जिनसे मैं बँधा हूँ, हे जातवेद। क्योंकि तुम्हारी इच्छा से ही — हम तुम्हारे सुमित्र हों।
verses.commentary: The culminating prayer of the Varuna sequence: "vimucenya si varuṇa pāśān" — release, O Varuna, the bonds. The Vedic concept of pāśa (bonds, fetters) — the same root that gives the word "pashu" (bound creature) in Shaiva Tantra. The bonds are not external chains but the interior constrictions produced by unresolved transgression: guilt, shame, the habitual contraction around what one has done or left undone. The prayer moves from "what did I do wrong?" (7.86.1) to "release the bonds" — acknowledging that whatever the transgression was, its effect is a constraint on life-force itself. "Sumitrāḥ syāma" — may we be your good friends. The relationship with the divine, having been fractured by transgression, seeks restoration.

verses.sanskrit: उषो देव्यमर्त्ये बृहद्वयो दधे | ज्योतिर्यच्छ चक्षसे ||
verses.transliteration: uṣo devyamartype bṛhadvayo dadhe | jyotiryaccha cakṣase ||
verses.translation: O divine Dawn, immortal one — grant great sustenance. Extend your light for our seeing.
verses.hindi: हे देवी उषस, अमर — महान पोषण प्रदान करो। हमारे देखने के लिए अपना प्रकाश फैलाओ।
verses.commentary: Ushas — the Dawn — is among the most philosophically rich figures in the Rig Veda. She is "amartye" — immortal, yet she appears and disappears daily. She is always new yet always the same. The hymn asks for two things together: "vayo" (sustenance, vitality, nourishment) and "jyotir cakṣase" (light for seeing). Not light as decoration — light as the precondition for perception. The connection is precise: without sustenance (physical, psychological, spiritual), the capacity to perceive clearly is diminished. The Dawn prayer is simultaneously a prayer for energy and for vision. Ushas as the Vedic archetype of renewal: every morning, without exception, regardless of what the previous night contained, the dawn comes. The universe itself demonstrates daily that darkness is not permanent.

verses.sanskrit: त्वामग्ने यजमाना अनु द्यून् विश्वा धियो अदधुः पुत्रमापेः | स नो मित्रो वरुणो मामहन्तामदितिः सिन्धुः पृथिवी उत द्यौः ||
verses.transliteration: tvāmagne yajamānā anu dyūn viśvā dhiyo adadhuḥ putramāpeḥ | sa no mitro varuṇo māmahantāmaditiḥ sindhuḥ pṛthivī uta dyauḥ ||
verses.translation: You, O Agni, the sacrificers throughout all days have placed as the child of the waters, the repository of all inspired visions. May Mitra, Varuna, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth and Heaven magnify us.
verses.hindi: हे अग्नि, यजमानों ने सभी दिनों में तुम्हें जलों के पुत्र के रूप में, सभी धियों (प्रेरित दर्शनों) के आधार के रूप में स्थापित किया है। मित्र, वरुण, अदिति, सिन्धु, पृथिवी और द्यौ हमें महान बनाएँ।
verses.commentary: The verse centres on "viśvā dhiyaḥ" — all the dhi, all the inspired visions. "Dhi" is one of the most important and untranslatable words in the Rig Veda: simultaneously meditative vision, inspired insight, illumined understanding, and the faculty that perceives truth directly rather than through inference. Agni is placed as the "repository of all dhi" — the sacred fire at the centre of the sacrifice is also the fire at the centre of the mind: the faculty of direct perception. The closing invocation brings together six cosmic powers — Mitra (covenant), Varuna (moral order), Aditi (boundless mother), Sindhu (the river, life-force), Earth, and Heaven — all asked to "magnify us." Not one god but the entire structure of cosmic reality as the context for human flourishing.

verses.sanskrit: इन्द्र क्रतुं न आ भर पितान आ भर | वसो पुरन्दर श्रुधी हवम् ||
verses.transliteration: indra kratuṃ na ā bhara pitā na ā bhara | vaso purandara śrudhī havam ||
verses.translation: O Indra, bring us purposeful will as a father brings. O master of abundance, destroyer of limitations — hear our call.
verses.hindi: हे इन्द्र, पिता की तरह हमें क्रतु (संकल्पशक्ति) लाओ। हे वसु (समृद्धि के स्वामी), पुरन्दर (बाधाओं के नाशक) — हमारी पुकार सुनो।
verses.commentary: "Kratuṃ na ā bhara pitā na" — bring us kratu as a father brings. The simile is precise: a father brings practical capacity to his children — not just love or intention but the actual functional ability to act effectively in the world. Kratu is purposeful will: not vague desire, not aspiration, but the integrated capacity of perception + intention + execution that allows a person to actually do what they know needs to be done. "Purandara" — the destroyer of puras (limitations, strongholds, the rigid structures that confine): Indra as the force that breaks through whatever has become too fixed, too defended, too calcified. The prayer asks Indra to break the internal strongholds — the habitual patterns, the defensive structures, the calcified beliefs — that prevent kratu from operating freely.

verses.transliteration: sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ sahasrākṣaḥ sahasrapāt | sa bhūmiṃ viśvato vṛtvātyatiṣṭhaddaśāṅgulam ||
verses.translation: The Cosmic Person has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet. He pervades the earth on all sides and stands ten fingers beyond.
verses.hindi: पुरुष (विराट्) के हज़ार सिर, हज़ार आँखें और हज़ार पैर हैं। वह सब ओर से पृथ्वी को व्याप्त करके दस अंगुल अतिक्रमण करके स्थित है।
verses.commentary: The Purusha Sukta (RV 10.90) presents the universe as a single vast Conscious Being — not as dead matter arranged by chance but as a living, integrated whole. "Thousand heads, eyes, feet" is not literal; it conveys omniscience, omnipresence, and infinite diversity within one consciousness. The universe is not a machine; it is a Person — aware, unified, complete.

verses.sanskrit: मरुतो यद्ध वो बलं यच्च सत्यमुत क्रतुः | तेन मा पातनाधसः ||
verses.transliteration: maruto yadha vo balaṃ yacca satyamuta kratuḥ | tena mā pātanādhasaḥ ||
verses.translation: O Maruts — whatever strength you have, whatever truth, whatever purposeful will — by that, protect me from falling low.
verses.hindi: हे मरुतो — तुम्हारे पास जो बल है, जो सत्य है, जो संकल्पशक्ति है — उससे मुझे नीचे गिरने से बचाओ।
verses.commentary: The Maruts are the storm-gods — the vital winds, the forces of prana that move through the cosmos and through the body. They are "bala" (strength), "satya" (truth), and "kratu" (purposeful will — the capacity to act with decisive intention). The prayer asks to be protected from "adhas" — falling low, sinking, degradation. The Maruts' three qualities are exactly what prevents that fall: physical vitality (bala) to sustain the body, truth (satya) to orient perception accurately, and purposeful will (kratu) to act from genuine intention rather than reactive impulse. The Vedic model of resilience: not the absence of storms but having the storm-energy itself as your ally.

verses.sanskrit: अपाम सोमममृता अभूमागन्म ज्योतिरविदाम देवान् | किं नूनमस्मान्कृणवदरातिः किमु धूर्तिरमृत मर्त्यस्य ||
verses.transliteration: apāma somamamṛtā abhūmāganma jyotiravadāma devān | kiṃ nūnamasmānkṛṇavadarātiḥ kimu dhūrtiraṃṛta martyasya ||
verses.translation: We have drunk Soma; we have become immortal; we have reached the light; we have found the gods. What can enmity do to us now? What can the malice of a mortal do, O Immortal?
verses.hindi: हमने सोम पिया है; हम अमर हो गए; हम प्रकाश को पहुँचे; हमने देवताओं को पाया। अब शत्रुता हमारा क्या कर सकती है? हे अमर, किसी मर्त्य की दुर्भावना क्या कर सकती है?
verses.commentary: RV 8.48 — the most celebrated verse of the entire Soma tradition and one of the most striking declarations in the Rig Veda. "Apāma somam amṛtā abhūma" — we have drunk Soma; we have become immortal. This is the experiential report of the Soma state: not a hope but a present-tense claim. "Āganma jyotir" — we have reached the light. The question that follows is the most confident in the Veda: "What can enmity do to us now?" The rhetorical answer: nothing. The state of illumined consciousness — however temporarily reached — reveals the relative smallness of what had seemed threatening. "Kimu dhūrtir amṛta martyasya" — what can the malice of a mortal do, O Immortal? Addressed to Soma: the purified consciousness is not invulnerable but it is no longer at the mercy of every external threat.

verses.transliteration: kiṃ ta āgaḥ varuṇa jyeṣṭhamāsa yo stotāraṃ jighāṃsasi sakhāyam | pra tanma indra varuṇa bravītaṃ yasminnenasyamasi jātavedasā ||
verses.translation: O Varuna, what was the greatest offence against you, that you would wish to harm your singer, your friend? Tell me, O Indra, O Varuna — in what sin am I involved, O Jataveda?
verses.hindi: हे वरुण, तुम्हारे विरुद्ध मेरा सबसे बड़ा अपराध क्या था जो तुम अपने स्तोता, अपने मित्र को हानि पहुँचाना चाहते हो? हे इन्द्र, हे वरुण — बताओ, मैं किस पाप में फँसा हूँ?
verses.commentary: RV 7.86 — the most psychologically raw prayer in the Rig Veda. Vasishtha addresses Varuna from a state of apparent illness or misfortune and asks: what sin did I commit? "Kiṃ ta āgaḥ" — what was my offence against you? The extraordinary quality: "yena enasyami" — in what sin am I involved — without knowing what it is. Not "I know my sin and confess it" but the experience of guilt without a clear object: the sense that something is wrong, that one has transgressed, without the ability to identify precisely what. Varuna, as omniscient guardian of Rita, knows what the supplicant does not. The prayer asks for both knowledge and forgiveness simultaneously — not absolution without understanding, but understanding followed by release.

verses.transliteration: mā no vadhīḥ varuṇa mā no hiṃsīr mā taṃ vadhīr yo naḥ priyaḥ | kṣayaṃ na indra varuṇa mṛtyor mā no dīrghāyuṣaḥ pāta ||
verses.translation: Slay us not, O Varuna; harm us not. Slay not him who is dear to us. Give us a home, O Indra-Varuna; guard us from death; protect us for long life.
verses.hindi: हे वरुण, हमें मत मारो, हमें हानि मत पहुँचाओ। जो हमें प्रिय है उसे मत मारो। हे इन्द्र-वरुण, हमें आश्रय दो; मृत्यु से हमारी रक्षा करो; दीर्घायु के लिए हमारी रक्षा करो।
verses.commentary: RV 7.89 — "Let me not yet, King Varuna, enter into the house of clay" — the most visceral of the Varuna hymns, and among the most human verses in the Rig Veda. "The house of clay" is the grave, the earth into which the body returns. The prayer is naked fear of death, brought directly to the god of moral order: I am not ready. Have mercy. The refrain "have mercy, spare me, Mighty Lord" runs through all five verses. verses.transliteration: ṛtasya panthā na dabhāya kiṃ cana vṛjinā hyasya naśyanti jantavaḥ | ṛtena dīrghamanu venato divaḥ padaṃ na duṣkṛte api taṃ naśe ||
verses.translation: The path of Rita cannot be deceived by anyone. Those who follow crooked ways perish. By Rita the vast luminous realm is reached — the evildoer cannot attain that place.

Not as divine punishment but as the natural consequence of acting against the structure of reality itself.

verses.translation: Indra moves in many forms through his powers of maya. His golden coursers are yoked a thousand and ten. They call him Shakra — may he who wins the heavenly light, lord of the good, be heroic.

Indra's māyā is his ability to appear in multiple forms simultaneously — the power of infinite self-expression. "Pururūpa" — many-formed. The thousand golden coursers are the infinite forces through which the cosmic principle of Indra manifests. This verse anticipates the Vedantic māyā doctrine: the one reality appears as the many through the creative power of self-differentiation.

verses.sanskrit: मरुतो यद्ध वो बलं यच्च सत्यमुत क्रतुः | तेन मा पातनाधसः ||
verses.transliteration: maruto yadha vo balaṃ yacca satyamuta kratuḥ | tena mā pātanādhasaḥ ||
verses.translation: O Maruts — whatever strength you have, whatever truth, whatever purposeful will — by that, protect me from falling low.
verses.hindi: हे मरुतो — तुम्हारे पास जो बल है, जो सत्य है, जो संकल्पशक्ति है — उससे मुझे नीचे गिरने से बचाओ।
verses.commentary: The Maruts are the storm-gods — the vital winds, the forces of prana that move through the cosmos and through the body. They are "bala" (strength), "satya" (truth), and "kratu" (purposeful will — the capacity to act with decisive intention). The prayer asks to be protected from "adhas" — falling low, sinking, degradation. The Maruts' three qualities are exactly what prevents that fall: physical vitality (bala) to sustain the body, truth (satya) to orient perception accurately, and purposeful will (kratu) to act from genuine intention rather than reactive impulse. The Vedic model of resilience: not the absence of storms but having the storm-energy itself as your ally.

verses.sanskrit: इन्द्र सखायं मा त्यक्तमस्मान् | स हि नः सखा प्रथमः ||
verses.transliteration: indra sakhāyaṃ mā tyaktamasmān | sa hi naḥ sakhā prathamaḥ ||
verses.translation: O Indra, do not abandon us, your friends. For you are our first and foremost companion.
verses.hindi: हे इन्द्र, हमें अपने मित्रों को मत त्यागो। क्योंकि तुम हमारे प्रथम और सर्वश्रेष्ठ सखा हो।
verses.commentary: "Sakhāyaṃ mā tyaktam" — do not abandon your friends. The Kanva poets address Indra with the intimacy of sakhi — friendship. This is theologically radical: not "do not abandon your worshippers" or "your servants" but "your friends." Friendship implies mutuality, reciprocity, genuine care. "Sa hi naḥ sakhā prathamaḥ" — you are our first and foremost sakha: Indra as the primary friendship, the foundational relationship from which all other relationships draw their meaning. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna calls himself Arjuna's sakha — the tradition traces directly back here. The divine as the friend who does not abandon — who is present in difficulty, not just in celebration.

verses.transliteration: apāma somamamṛtā abhūmāganma jyotiravadāma devān | kiṃ nūnamasmānkṛṇavadarātiḥ kimu dhūrtiraṃṛta martyasya ||
verses.translation: We have drunk Soma; we have become immortal; we have reached the light; we have found the gods. What can enmity do to us now? What can the malice of a mortal do, O Immortal?
verses.hindi: हमने सोम पिया है; हम अमर हो गए; हम प्रकाश को पहुँचे; हमने देवताओं को पाया। अब शत्रुता हमारा क्या कर सकती है? हे अमर, किसी मर्त्य की दुर्भावना क्या कर सकती है?
verses.commentary: RV 8.48 — the most celebrated verse of the entire Soma tradition and one of the most striking declarations in the Rig Veda. "Apāma somam amṛtā abhūma" — we have drunk Soma; we have become immortal. This is the experiential report of the Soma state: not a hope but a present-tense claim. "Āganma jyotir" — we have reached the light. The question that follows is the most confident in the Veda: "What can enmity do to us now?" The rhetorical answer: nothing. The state of illumined consciousness — however temporarily reached — reveals the relative smallness of what had seemed threatening. "Kimu dhūrtir amṛta martyasya" — what can the malice of a mortal do, O Immortal? Addressed to Soma: the purified consciousness is not invulnerable but it is no longer at the mercy of every external threat.

verses.transliteration: sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ sahasrākṣaḥ sahasrapāt | sa bhūmiṃ viśvato vṛtvātyatiṣṭhaddaśāṅgulam ||
verses.translation: The Cosmic Person has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet. He pervades the earth on all sides and stands ten fingers beyond.
verses.hindi: पुरुष (विराट्) के हज़ार सिर, हज़ार आँखें और हज़ार पैर हैं। वह सब ओर से पृथ्वी को व्याप्त करके दस अंगुल अतिक्रमण करके स्थित है।
verses.commentary: The Purusha Sukta (RV 10.90) presents the universe as a single vast Conscious Being — not as dead matter arranged by chance but as a living, integrated whole. "Thousand heads, eyes, feet" is not literal; it conveys omniscience, omnipresence, and infinite diversity within one consciousness. The universe is not a machine; it is a Person — aware, unified, complete.

verses.translation: O Maruts — whatever strength you have, whatever truth, whatever purposeful will — by that, protect me from falling low.
verses.hindi: हे मरुतो — तुम्हारे पास जो बल है, जो सत्य है, जो संकल्पशक्ति है — उससे मुझे नीचे गिरने से बचाओ।
verses.commentary: The Maruts are the storm-gods — the vital winds, the forces of prana that move through the cosmos and through the body. They are "bala" (strength), "satya" (truth), and "kratu" (purposeful will — the capacity to act with decisive intention). The prayer asks to be protected from "adhas" — falling low, sinking, degradation. The Maruts' three qualities are exactly what prevents that fall: physical vitality (bala) to sustain the body, truth (satya) to orient perception accurately, and purposeful will (kratu) to act from genuine intention rather than reactive impulse. The Vedic model of resilience: not the absence of storms but having the storm-energy itself as your ally.

verses.sanskrit: इन्द्र क्रतुं न आ भर पितान आ भर | वसो पुरन्दर श्रुधी हवम् ||
verses.transliteration: indra kratuṃ na ā bhara pitā na ā bhara | vaso purandara śrudhī havam ||
verses.translation: O Indra, bring us purposeful will as a father brings. O master of abundance, destroyer of limitations — hear our call.
verses.hindi: हे इन्द्र, पिता की तरह हमें क्रतु (संकल्पशक्ति) लाओ। हे वसु (समृद्धि के स्वामी), पुरन्दर (बाधाओं के नाशक) — हमारी पुकार सुनो।
verses.commentary: "Kratuṃ na ā bhara pitā na" — bring us kratu as a father brings. The simile is precise: a father brings practical capacity to his children — not just love or intention but the actual functional ability to act effectively in the world. Kratu is purposeful will: not vague desire, not aspiration, but the integrated capacity of perception + intention + execution that allows a person to actually do what they know needs to be done. "Purandara" — the destroyer of puras (limitations, strongholds, the rigid structures that confine): Indra as the force that breaks through whatever has become too fixed, too defended, too calcified. The prayer asks Indra to break the internal strongholds — the habitual patterns, the defensive structures, the calcified beliefs — that prevent kratu from operating freely.

verses.sanskrit: पवमानः सोमो अद्य नो देवेभ्यः पाहि | तरणिर्विश्वदर्शतो ज्योतिष्कृदसि सोम ||
verses.transliteration: pavamānaḥ somo adya no devebhyaḥ pāhi | taraṇirviśvadarśato jyotiṣkṛdasi soma ||
verses.translation: O Soma Pavamana, protect us today for the gods. You are swift, all-seeing, O Soma — you are the maker of light.
verses.hindi: हे सोम पवमान, आज हमारी देवताओं के लिए रक्षा करो। हे सोम, तुम तीव्रगामी हो, सर्वदर्शी हो — तुम प्रकाश के निर्माता हो।
verses.commentary: The opening invocation of Mandala 9. "Pavamāna" — the purifying one, the one who flows through the filter: the central epithet of Soma in this Mandala. Every element of the Soma ritual was simultaneously a symbol of inner purification. "Taraṇiḥ" — swift, the one who carries across: Soma as the vehicle that ferries the supplicant across obstacles. "Viśvadarśataḥ" — all-seeing: Soma as the state of expanded, purified perception that sees what ordinarily contracted consciousness cannot. "Jyotiṣkṛt" — maker of light: the purified consciousness generates its own luminosity. Purification does not add light from outside — it removes the obstruction to the light that is already present.

verses.sanskrit: अभि त्वा देव सवितरीशानं वार्याणां सोम राजन्नमृतस्य भूरेः | इन्दुमिन्द्राय पवस्व ||
verses.transliteration: abhi tvā deva savitarīśānaṃ vāryāṇāṃ soma rājannamṛtasya bhūreḥ | indumindrasya pavasva ||
verses.translation: O divine Savitar, lord of desirable things — O King Soma, purify for Indra the drop that contains the abundance of immortality.
verses.hindi: हे देव सवितर, वांछनीय वस्तुओं के स्वामी — हे सोम राज, अमृत की प्रचुरता को समेटे उस बूँद को इन्द्र के लिए शुद्ध करो।
verses.commentary: One of the Soma Mandala's most concentrated verses: "indumindrasya pavasva" — purify the drop (indu) for Indra. The "indu" — the drop, the single point — is simultaneously the individual drop of Soma, the individual soul (jivatman), and the concentrated point of awareness in meditation. The drop contains "amṛtasya bhūreḥ" — the abundance of immortality. The single drop already contains infinity. Purification does not add anything to it — it removes what obscures what is already there. This is the Soma Mandala's most direct teaching: you already contain what you are seeking. Purification is the process of uncovering it, not acquiring it.

verses.sanskrit: सहस्रशीर्षा पुरुषः सहस्राक्षः सहस्रपात् | स भूमिं विश्वतो वृत्वात्यतिष्ठद्दशाङ्गुलम् ||
verses.transliteration: sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ sahasrākṣaḥ sahasrapāt | sa bhūmiṃ viśvato vṛtvātyatiṣṭhaddaśāṅgulam ||
verses.translation: The Cosmic Person has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet. He pervades the earth on all sides and stands ten fingers beyond.
verses.hindi: पुरुष (विराट्) के हज़ार सिर, हज़ार आँखें और हज़ार पैर हैं। वह सब ओर से पृथ्वी को व्याप्त करके दस अंगुल अतिक्रमण करके स्थित है।
verses.commentary: The Purusha Sukta (RV 10.90) presents the universe as a single vast Conscious Being — not as dead matter arranged by chance but as a living, integrated whole. "Thousand heads, eyes, feet" is not literal; it conveys omniscience, omnipresence, and infinite diversity within one consciousness. The universe is not a machine; it is a Person — aware, unified, complete.

verses.sanskrit: विमुचेन्यसि वरुण पाशान् यैरबद्धो असि जातवेदः | यद्धि ते विश्वमनुमत्यम्भिर्वयं सुमित्राः स्याम ||
verses.transliteration: vimucenya si varuṇa pāśān yairabaddho asi jātavedaḥ | yaddhi te viśvamanumatyambhirvayaṃ sumitrāḥ syāma ||
verses.translation: Release, O Varuna, the bonds with which I am bound, O Jataveda. For by your will, O all-knowing one — may we be among your good friends.
verses.hindi: हे वरुण, उन बन्धनों से मुझे मुक्त करो जिनसे मैं बँधा हूँ, हे जातवेद। क्योंकि तुम्हारी इच्छा से ही — हम तुम्हारे सुमित्र हों।
verses.commentary: The culminating prayer of the Varuna sequence: "vimucenya si varuṇa pāśān" — release, O Varuna, the bonds. The Vedic concept of pāśa (bonds, fetters) — the same root that gives the word "pashu" (bound creature) in Shaiva Tantra. The bonds are not external chains but the interior constrictions produced by unresolved transgression: guilt, shame, the habitual contraction around what one has done or left undone. The prayer moves from "what did I do wrong?" (7.86.1) to "release the bonds" — acknowledging that whatever the transgression was, its effect is a constraint on life-force itself. "Sumitrāḥ syāma" — may we be your good friends. The relationship with the divine, having been fractured by transgression, seeks restoration.

verses.sanskrit: ऋतस्य पन्था न दभाय किं चन वृजिना ह्यस्य नश्यन्ति जन्तवः | ऋतेन दीर्घमनु वेनतो दिवः पदं न दुष्कृते अपि तं नशे ||
verses.transliteration: ṛtasya panthā na dabhāya kiṃ cana vṛjinā hyasya naśyanti jantavaḥ | ṛtena dīrghamanu venato divaḥ padaṃ na duṣkṛte api taṃ naśe ||
verses.translation: The path of Rita cannot be deceived by anyone. Those who follow crooked ways perish. By Rita the vast luminous realm is reached — the evildoer cannot attain that place.
verses.hindi: ऋत के मार्ग को कोई धोखा नहीं दे सकता। वक्र पथ पर चलने वाले नष्ट हो जाते हैं। ऋत से ही वह विशाल द्युलोक प्राप्त होता है — दुष्कर्मी उसे नहीं पा सकता।
verses.commentary: The Rig Veda's most direct statement of Rita — the cosmic ordering principle that is simultaneously physical law and moral law. "Ṛtasya panthā na dabhāya kiṃ cana" — the path of cosmic order cannot be deceived by anyone. Gravity does not make exceptions. Truth does not make exceptions. Rita maintains the three worlds — earth, atmosphere, heaven. The moral implication: human actions that conform to Rita produce flourishing; those that violate it produce destruction. Not as divine punishment but as the natural consequence of acting against the structure of reality itself.

verses.sanskrit: इन्द्रो मायाभिः पुरुरूप ईयते युक्ता ह्यस्य हरयः शता दश | आयं शक्र इत्येनमाहुर्यः स्वर्षाता सत्पतिः शूरो अस्तु ||
verses.transliteration: indro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate yuktā hyasya harayaḥ śatā daśa | āyaṃ śakra ityenamāhuryaḥ svarṣātā satpatiḥ śūro astu ||
verses.translation: Indra moves in many forms through his powers of maya. His golden coursers are yoked a thousand and ten. They call him Shakra — may he who wins the heavenly light, lord of the good, be heroic.
verses.hindi: इन्द्र अपनी माया-शक्तियों से अनेक रूप धारण करके विचरते हैं। उनके दस सौ सुनहरे अश्व जुते हैं। उन्हें शक्र कहते हैं — जो स्वर्ग-प्रकाश प्राप्त करे, सत्पुरुषों का स्वामी, वह शूर हो।
verses.commentary: This verse introduces one of the Rig Veda's most philosophically rich concepts: Vedic "māyā" — not yet in its later Vedantic sense of "illusion" but in its original sense of "creative power, the capacity to take many forms." Indra's māyā is his ability to appear in multiple forms simultaneously — the power of infinite self-expression. "Pururūpa" — many-formed. The thousand golden coursers are the infinite forces through which the cosmic principle of Indra manifests. This verse anticipates the Vedantic māyā doctrine: the one reality appears as the many through the creative power of self-differentiation.

verses.sanskrit: अपाम सोमममृता अभूमागन्म ज्योतिरविदाम देवान् | किं नूनमस्मान्कृणवदरातिः किमु धूर्तिरमृत मर्त्यस्य ||
verses.transliteration: apāma somamamṛtā abhūmāganma jyotiravadāma devān | kiṃ nūnamasmānkṛṇavadarātiḥ kimu dhūrtiraṃṛta martyasya ||
verses.translation: We have drunk Soma; we have become immortal; we have reached the light; we have found the gods. What can enmity do to us now? What can the malice of a mortal do, O Immortal?
verses.hindi: हमने सोम पिया है; हम अमर हो गए; हम प्रकाश को पहुँचे; हमने देवताओं को पाया। अब शत्रुता हमारा क्या कर सकती है? हे अमर, किसी मर्त्य की दुर्भावना क्या कर सकती है?
verses.commentary: RV 8.48 — the most celebrated verse of the entire Soma tradition and one of the most striking declarations in the Rig Veda. "Apāma somam amṛtā abhūma" — we have drunk Soma; we have become immortal. This is the experiential report of the Soma state: not a hope but a present-tense claim. "Āganma jyotir" — we have reached the light. The question that follows is the most confident in the Veda: "What can enmity do to us now?" The rhetorical answer: nothing. The state of illumined consciousness — however temporarily reached — reveals the relative smallness of what had seemed threatening. "Kimu dhūrtir amṛta martyasya" — what can the malice of a mortal do, O Immortal? Addressed to Soma: the purified consciousness is not invulnerable but it is no longer at the mercy of every external threat.

verses.sanskrit: नासदासीन्नो सदासीत्तदानीं नासीद्रजो नो व्योमा परो यत् | किमावरीवः कुह कस्य शर्मन्नम्भः किमासीद्गहनं गभीरम् ||
verses.transliteration: nāsadāsīnno sadāsīttadānīṃ nāsīdrajo no vyomā paro yat | kimāvarīvaḥ kuha kasya śarmannambhaḥ kimāsīdgahanaṃ gabhīram ||
verses.translation: Neither existence nor non-existence was there then; neither sky nor heaven beyond. What stirred? Where? Under whose shelter? Was there deep, unfathomable water?
verses.hindi: उस समय न सत् था, न असत् था; न आकाश था, न उसके परे कुछ था। क्या आच्छादित था? कहाँ? किसके शरण में? क्या अथाह जल था?
verses.commentary: The Nasadiya Sukta (RV 10.129) is one of the most remarkable philosophical poems ever written. It asks: before the universe existed, what was there? Its answer is deliberately agnostic — not "God created it" but honest inquiry. It oscillates between sat (existence) and asat (non-existence), unable to place the primordial state in either category. This intellectual honesty — saying "we don't know" — is extraordinary for a text 3500 years old.

verses.sanskrit: को अद्धा वेद क इह प्र वोचत् कुत आजाता कुत इयं विसृष्टिः | अर्वाग्देवा अस्य विसर्जनेनाथा को वेद यत आबभूव ||
verses.transliteration: ko addhā veda ka iha pra vocat kuta ājātā kuta iyaṃ visṛṣṭiḥ | arvāgdevā asya visarjanena athā ko veda yata ābabhūva ||
verses.translation: Who really knows? Who will here proclaim it? From where was it born, from where this creation? The gods came after this world's creation — so who knows from where it came into being?
verses.hindi: कौन वास्तव में जानता है? यहाँ कौन बता सकता है? यह कहाँ से उत्पन्न हुआ? यह सृष्टि कहाँ से आई? देवता इस सृष्टि के बाद आए — तो फिर कौन जानता है यह कहाँ से उत्पन्न हुई?
verses.commentary: The Nasadiya Sukta ends without answering its own questions. Even the gods don't know — they came after creation. Perhaps not even the one who surveys all from the highest heaven knows. This is one of the most honest intellectual positions in all of ancient literature. The Vedic rishi chose the integrity of "I don't know" over the comfort of a confident creation myth.

verses.sanskrit: सहस्रशीर्षा पुरुषः सहस्राक्षः सहस्रपात् | स भूमिं विश्वतो वृत्वात्यतिष्ठद्दशाङ्गुलम् ||
verses.transliteration: sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ sahasrākṣaḥ sahasrapāt | sa bhūmiṃ viśvato vṛtvātyatiṣṭhaddaśāṅgulam ||
verses.translation: The Cosmic Person has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet. He pervades the earth on all sides and stands ten fingers beyond.
verses.hindi: पुरुष (विराट्) के हज़ार सिर, हज़ार आँखें और हज़ार पैर हैं। वह सब ओर से पृथ्वी को व्याप्त करके दस अंगुल अतिक्रमण करके स्थित है।
verses.commentary: The Purusha Sukta (RV 10.90) presents the universe as a single vast Conscious Being — not as dead matter arranged by chance but as a living, integrated whole. "Thousand heads, eyes, feet" is not literal; it conveys omniscience, omnipresence, and infinite diversity within one consciousness. The universe is not a machine; it is a Person — aware, unified, complete.

verses.sanskrit: तपसा चीयते ब्रह्म ततो अन्नमभिजायते | अन्नात्प्राणो जायते मनः सत्यं च जायते ||
verses.transliteration: tapasā cīyate brahma tato annamabhijāyate | annātprāṇo jāyate manaḥ satyaṃ ca jāyate ||
verses.translation: Through Tapas, Brahma increases. From that, food is born. From food, Prana is born. From Prana, mind and truth are born.
verses.hindi: तप से ब्रह्म बढ़ता है; उससे अन्न उत्पन्न होता है; अन्न से प्राण उत्पन्न होता है; प्राण से मन और सत्य उत्पन्न होते हैं।
verses.commentary: RV 10.190 — the Tapas creation hymn. Griffith translates the opening of this hymn: "From Fervour kindled to its height, Eternal Law and Truth were born: thence was the Night produced, and thence the billowy flood of sea arose." Tapas — translated as fervour, heat, creative austerity — is the foundational creative principle of this hymn: not a creator-god who wills the universe into being, but a self-intensifying heat that produces reality through its own excess. The cosmological sequence given here is simultaneously a map of the human being. Tapas (disciplined practice, sustained effort, willing engagement with difficulty) → Brahma (the expansive principle, widened awareness) → Anna (food, matter, the physical foundation) → Prana (vital force, life-energy) → Manas (mind) → Satya (truth-perception). The universe was created in this sequence. The human being develops in this same sequence. The creation of the cosmos and the cultivation of wisdom follow identical laws.

verses.sanskrit: योगश्चित्तवृत्तिरोधो योगो मोक्षप्रदायकः | योगः सर्वबन्धानां योगो ब्रह्मसमाश्रयः ||
verses.transliteration: yogaścittavṛttirodho yogo mokṣapradāyakaḥ | yogaḥ sarvabandhānāṃ yogaḥ brahmasamāśrayaḥ ||
verses.translation: Yoga is the cessation of mental modifications; yoga gives liberation. Yoga cuts all bonds; yoga rests on Brahman.
verses.hindi: योग चित्त-वृत्तियों का निरोध है; योग मोक्ष देता है। योग सभी बंधनों को काटता है; योग ब्रह्म पर आश्रित है।
verses.commentary: The definition of yoga from Yoga Sutras, placed in the context of Brahman. Yoga is the cessation of mental modifications, leading to liberation. All bonds are cut through this practice, which rests on the foundation of Brahman.
verses.wordMeaning: The definition of yoga from Yoga Sutras, placed in the context of Brahman. Yoga is the cessation of mental modifications, leading to liberation. All bonds are cut through this practice, which rests on the foundation of Brahman.

verses.sanskrit: अहं ब्रह्मास्मि न त्वं भूतिर्न च भूतानि | सर्वं ब्रह्म एव सर्वं ब्रह्म मयि सर्वम् ||
verses.transliteration: ahaṃ brahmāsmi na tvaṃ bhūtirna ca bhūtāni | sarvaṃ brahma eva sarvaṃ brahma mayi sarvam ||
verses.translation: I am Brahman, not you; I am birth, not beings; all is Brahman alone, all is Brahman in me.
verses.hindi: मैं ब्रह्म हूँ, तुम नहीं; मैं जन्म हूँ, प्राणी नहीं; सब ब्रह्म ही है, सब ब्रह्म मेरे में है।
verses.commentary: The declaration of non-duality with Brahman as the supreme. The individual Self is Brahman; the world is Brahman; all distinctions dissolve in this recognition.
verses.wordMeaning: The declaration of non-duality with Brahman as the supreme. The individual Self is Brahman; the world is Brahman; all distinctions dissolve in this recognition.

verses.sanskrit: यथा नदी समुद्रेषु यथा दीपो दीतेषु | तथा जीवो ब्रह्मणि लीनो न तत्र संशयो भवति ||
verses.transliteration: yathā nadī samudreṣu yathā dīpo dīpiteṣu | tathā jīvo brahmaṇi līno na tatra saṃśayo bhavati ||
verses.translation: As rivers merge into the ocean, as lamps merge into light — so the individual self merges into Brahman. There is no doubt about this.
verses.hindi: जैसे नदियाँ समुद्र में लीन हो जाती हैं, जैसे दीप ज्योति में लीन हो जाते हैं — वैसे ही जीव ब्रह्म में लीन हो जाता है। इसमें कोई संशय नहीं।
verses.commentary: The dissolution of individuality into Brahman. The images of rivers into ocean and lamps into light illustrate the loss of separate identity while the essence remains.
verses.wordMeaning: The dissolution of individuality into Brahman. The images of rivers into ocean and lamps into light illustrate the loss of separate identity while the essence remains.

verses.sanskrit: शान्तं शिवमद्वैतं ब्रह्म नित्यं शुद्धमच्युतम् | यो जानाति स पश्यति यो न जानाति न पश्यति ||
verses.transliteration: śāntaṃ śivamadvaitaṃ brahma nityaṃ śuddhamacyutam | yo jānāti sa paśyati yo na jānāti na paśyati ||
verses.translation: Peaceful, auspicious, non-dual Brahman — eternal, pure, immutable. He who knows, sees; he who does not know, does not see.
verses.hindi: शांत, शिव, अद्वैत ब्रह्म — नित्य, शुद्ध, अच्युत। जो जानता है, वह देखता है; जो नहीं जानता, वह नहीं देखता।
verses.commentary: The attributes of Brahman: peaceful, auspicious, non-dual, eternal, pure, immutable. Knowledge is seeing; ignorance is blindness.
verses.wordMeaning: The attributes of Brahman: peaceful, auspicious, non-dual, eternal, pure, immutable. Knowledge is seeing; ignorance is blindness.

verses.sanskrit: एको देवो द्वितीयो नास्ति यो ब्रह्म वेद तत्त्वतः | सोऽहमस्मि न किंचिद्भूतो न मृत्युर्न शोको न तथा ||
verses.transliteration: eko devo dvitīyo nāsti yo brahma veda tattvataḥ | so'hamasmi na kiñcidbhūto na mṛtyurna śoko na tathā ||
verses.translation: There is one God, no second — he who knows Brahman in truth. I am He, not any being, no death, no sorrow, and so on.
verses.hindi: एक ही देव है, दूसरा कोई नहीं — जो ब्रह्म को तत्व से जानता है। मैं वही हूँ, कोई प्राणी नहीं, मृत्यु नहीं, शोक नहीं, वगैरह।
verses.commentary: The affirmation of non-duality: one reality, no second. The knower recognizes "I am He" and transcends death, sorrow, and all suffering.
verses.wordMeaning: The affirmation of non-duality: one reality, no second. The knower recognizes "I am He" and transcends death, sorrow, and all suffering.

verses.sanskrit: एकं सत् विप्रा बहुधा वदन्ति | अग्निं यमं मातरिश्वानमाहुः | दिव्यं देवानग्निं गृहपतिं | यज्ञियं यज्ञसाधनमाहुः ||
verses.transliteration: ekaṃ sat viprā bahudhā vadanti | agniṃ yamaṃ mātariśvānāmāhuḥ | divyaṃ devānagniṃ gṛhapatiṃ | yajñiyam yajñasādhanamāhuḥ ||
verses.translation: The wise speak of what is one in many ways — they call it Agni, Yama, Matarishvan. Divine is Agni, the god of gods, the lord of the house, the worthy one, the fulfiller of sacrifice.
verses.hindi: विद्वान एक को अनेक रूपों में कहते हैं — उसे अग्नि, यम, मातरिश्वन कहते हैं। दिव्य अग्नि है, देवों का देव, गृहपति, यज्ञिय, यज्ञ का साधक।ा।
verses.commentary: RV 1.164.46 — one of the most famous verses in the Rig Veda, often cited as the earliest statement of non-duality. "Ekaṃ sat" — the truth is one. The wise describe it in many ways. The same reality is called Agni (fire), Yama (death/dharma), Matarishvan (wind). This is not polytheism but recognition that the one reality has multiple names and forms. The Rig Veda already contains the seed of the later Vedantic teaching: ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti.

verses.sanskrit: अग्निमीळे पुरोहितं यज्ञस्य देवमृत्विजम् | होतारं रत्नधातमम् ||
verses.transliteration: agnimīḷe purohitaṃ yajñasya devamṛtavijam | hotāraṃ ratnadhātamam ||
verses.translation: I invoke Agni, the priest, the sacrificer of the sacrifice, the divine minister of truth, the bestower of treasures.
verses.hindi: अग्नि को आह्वान करता हूँ — पुरोहित, यज्ञ का यज्ञक, दिव्य ऋत्विज, रत्न देने वाला।
verses.commentary: The opening verse of the Rig Veda (RV 1.1.1) — the first verse of the entire Vedic corpus. Agni is invoked as the priest who conducts the sacrifice, but also as the sacrifice itself. This is the foundational verse of all Vedic tradition: fire as the mediator between the human and the divine, the purifier, the transformer. Agni is not merely physical fire but the principle of transformation itself.

verses.sanskrit: असतो मा सद्गमय तसो मा द्विर्मा यो रदस्ति नियोऽस्तु नः | येन देवाः सयमन्ता उपास्ये नव्येन मध्यमा नव्येन समाध्याता ||
verses.transliteration: asato mā sadgamaya tamasomā jyotirgamayo mṛtyormā amṛtaṃ gamaya | śrīrno mā bhavati rādhasīrno bhūtā mā bhūyāsmaḥ | yenadevāḥ sayamantā upāsye navīena madhyamā navīena samādhyātā ||
verses.translation: From untruth lead us to truth; from darkness lead us to light; from death lead us to immortality. May we not be separated from glory; may we not be separated from merit. May we be united with the divine through meditation.
verses.hindi: असत से सत की ओर ले चलो; अंधकार से प्रकाश की ओर ले चलो; मृत्यु से अमृत की ओर ले चलो। हमें यश से न अलग होने दो; पुण्य से न अलग होने दो। देवों के साथ ध्यान से जुड़ने दो।
verses.commentary: The famous Asatoma mantra from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, deeply rooted in Vedic tradition. Three great invocations: asat to sat (untruth to truth), tamas to jyoti (darkness to light), mrityu to amrita (death to immortality). This is the Vedic prayer for transformation — not asking for material gain but for fundamental shift of being. The Rig Veda contains the seed of this prayer in its fire hymns and invocations.

verses.sanskrit: श्रद्धावान् लभते ज्ञानम् अश्रद्धान् न लभते | ज्ञानात् यथा योगः सिद्धिः सर्वभूतेषु तथा ||
verses.transliteration: śraddhāvān labhate jñānam aśraddhān na labhate | jñānāt yathā yogaḥ siddhiḥ sarvabhūteṣu tathā ||
verses.translation: The faithful attain knowledge; the faithless do not. From knowledge comes perfection (yoga) in all beings.
verses.hindi: श्रद्धावान ज्ञान प्राप्त करता है; अश्रद्धान नहीं। ज्ञान से सिद्धि आती है — सभी प्राणियों में।
verses.commentary: The Rig Veda identifies shraddha (faith, trust, sincere commitment) as the prerequisite for knowledge. Not intellectual capacity, not intelligence, not effort alone — but shraddha. Faith here is not blind belief but sincere openness to the possibility of truth. Without that openness, knowledge cannot be received. With it, the result is siddhi — perfection, yoga, integration in all dimensions of life.

verses.sanskrit: यज्ञेन यज्ञमयजन्त देवाः | तानि धर्माणि प्रथमान्यासन् | ते नो अदित्यान्मनुष्याः पूर्वे | साक्षादाग्रे प्रतिष्ठिता ||
verses.transliteration: yajñena yajñamayajanta devāḥ | tāni dharmāṇi prathamānyāsan | te no adityānmanuṣyāḥ pūrve | sākṣādāgre pratiṣṭhitā ||
verses.translation: The gods performed sacrifice through sacrifice. These were the first dharmas. These dharmas reached the humans of ancient times — established in the beginning, visible.
verses.hindi: देवों ने यज्ञ से यज्ञ किया। ये प्रथम धर्म थे। वे पुराने मनुष्यों तक पहुँचे — आदि में स्थापित, साक्षात दृष्ट।
verses.commentary: RV 10.90.16 — the Purusha Sukta continues with this verse about sacrifice. The gods themselves performed sacrifice to attain their status. This establishes yajna (sacrifice, offering, self-giving) as the fundamental cosmic principle. The dharmas established through sacrifice are the oldest and most reliable principles of human life. The Rig Veda teaches that sacrifice is not merely ritual but the structural principle of reality itself.
